en: The *Dharmapada-gāthā-saṃgraha-sūtra*, Chapter One:
On Conditioned Phenomena (*Saṃskṛta-varga*), compiled by the Venerable Dharmatrāta in Jalandhara, Central India.
1. This Chapter on the Conditioned can awaken one from the afflictions;
you should give rise to a heart of joy and now listen to the verses of the Dharma proclaimed by the Buddha, which I have compiled.
Thus the Buddha, the World-Honored One, the Teacher among those of all-knowledge, out of compassion for sentient beings, has extensively proclaimed these words of truth:
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are all subject to arising and passing away."
Life inevitably returns to its end; nirvāṇa is the supreme peace and joy.
Like a candle burning brightly when an object is cast into darkness, if one does not seek the lamp of wisdom, one will forever be shrouded by afflictions.
The human body has a physical form, yet it is cast away and scattered in all directions;
its bones turn the color of a pigeon—observing this, what joy is there?
Just as at the first watch of night, consciousness takes up residence within the mother’s womb.
Daily we encounter many shifts and changes; once gone, they are fixed and do not return.
What appears as a pleasant thing in the morning is no longer visible by night;
what was beheld yesterday may be absent this evening.
Glory and wealth may blaze with intense splendor, yet impermanence knows no season;
it makes no distinction between noble and base, for all are constantly subject to the King of Death.
Some perish within the womb, while others die at the very moment of birth.
In the prime of youth one cannot avoid death; in old age and decrepitude, one accepts it with resignation.
Whether one be old, young, or in middle age, all are constantly assailed by death; how can one not harbor fear?
Life is like fruit ripening on its own; one always fears it will fall away.
Since birth there must be an end, who can escape this?
It is like a potter who kneads clay to fashion earthen vessels.
All things are subject to destruction; the life of a human being is just like this.
It is like a person playing the lute or the harp, complete with all its exquisite sounds;
when the strings break, there is not even a slight sound left. The life of a human being is just like this.
Like a prisoner bound in fetters, Dragged along toward the marketplace,
Every movement leads toward the path of death— Such is the nature of life.
Like the swift current of a river, Which flows on and never returns.
Human life is likewise: that which has passed away never returns.
All manner of afflictions accumulate within this body; birth brings forth manifold suffering and distress.
The life of a person is also like this, ever watched by old age and death.
The merit accomplished through one's efforts brings peace and happiness for all eternity;
yet it is like striking swift water with a staff—it briefly parts and then closes back together again.
It is like a person holding a staff while walking, tending cattle and feeding them.
Human life is also like this; it proceeds while one sustains it.
If a person wishes to establish virtue, they must not let day or night pass in vain.
Having already obtained this human body, one should focus the mind on the end of life.
For one who cannot sleep, the night is long; for the weary, the road is long;
for the ignorant and deluded, birth and death are long. Thus, one longs to hear the Sublime Dharma.
When one possesses both children and wealth, yet encounters their loss through stinginess and attachment, they are utterly destroyed.
The fool does not examine himself; on what can he rely, having wealth and sons?
Though numbering in the hundreds of thousands beyond calculation—men and women of noble lineage and great riches—there are none whose accumulated property does not eventually decay and perish.
Wealth and nobility are not the treasures of the noble; they are constantly shadowed by impermanence.
Like a person who is blind, one cannot observe for oneself.
What is gathered must eventually disperse and decay; what is lofty will inevitably fall.
All who are born must come to an end; sentient beings are likewise so.
Those who commit evil enter hell; those who cultivate goodness are born in heaven.
If one can cultivate goodness, one will exhaust the outflows and attain nirvana.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, the Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas, even relinquish their conditioned bodies; how much more so should all sentient beings?
Neither in the sky nor in the midst of the ocean, nor by entering mountain caves, can one escape death.
There is no place on earth where one can dwell in safety and escape death.
Whether abiding in the present, the past, or the future,
all conditioned phenomena ultimately end in decay and destruction.
The wise one is able to sever all fetters, Constantly observing with right mindfulness, Always contemplating the untainted path; Such a person is called a true wise one.
Like a prisoner bound in shackles, What they desire can bring no benefit.
Just like a dilapidated old cart, it will soon be seen falling apart.
Physical form changes into decrepitude; attached to home as if in prison, one fails to perceive the arrival of death—the fool cannot know this.
Though one may live a full hundred years, one is nonetheless followed by death;
oppressed by old age and illness, suffering ultimately reaches its final limit.
When old age arrives, the body is entangled in misery, with much pain and affliction day and night.
Though there be a thousand kinds of bitter suffering, like a fish cast into ash and fire;
as rivers never cease their flow, rushing currents that go forth and do not return—
though one cherishes this pus-leaking body and clings to it with longing, it cannot remain.
This body is a collection of the four great elements; impermanent, how could it remain for long?
When the earth-element disperses and disintegrates, what use is the empty consciousness?
This body is full of obstacles and afflictions; it constantly leaks pus and is plagued by disease.
Deluded by ignorance and attached through craving, they do not weary of seeking nirvana.
Though this year is said to still exist, winter and summer will not linger long;
yet ordinary beings crave worldly pleasures and feel no alarm during the interval.
Parents and brothers, wives and kinsmen—
when impermanence draws them away, none can provide rescue.
Thus all sentient beings, in their every movement, crave honor and pleasure.
Impermanence, old age, and sickness assail; one does not realize that suffering arises.
Having shaved your head to become a bhikṣu, you ought to cultivate śamatha and vipaśyanā.
Then Māra will be unable to find an opportunity, and you shall deliver sentient beings to the other shore.
I know the root of your desire: it arises from mental conceptualization.
If I do not engage in such conceptualization, then your desire will not exist.
From desire arise afflictions; from desire arise fears.
Through detachment from desire one attains liberation; there is no fear and no affliction.
From craving arise afflictions; from craving arises fear.
Through detachment from craving one attains liberation; there is no fear and no affliction.
Fruit is sweet at first but bitter in the end; sensual desire is just like this.
Later one undergoes the suffering of hell, being burned and boiled for countless eons.
Foolish and deluded, they crave and lust after desires, becoming attached to wives and children.
Bound by the fetters of craving and passion, it is firm and difficult to escape.
The Noble Ones demonstrate that while love and desire adorn one's retinue,
it is the renunciation of wife and children that is truly firm and beneficial.
Craving is difficult to liberate from; leaving desire behind is true renunciation.
Not craving, one experiences happiness; the wise have no desires.
Those in the world who crave harbor all manner of improper thoughts.
If one can subdue [the mind], this is called true detachment from desire.
If a person constantly craves desire, they remain bound and find it difficult to be liberated.
Only through wisdom can one discern [reality], so that afflictions are severed and do not arise again.
Right mindfulness constantly arises; tranquility makes desire easy to remove.
Self-restraint through the Dharma-precepts prevents transgression, and goodness increases.
Those who constantly practice sensual desire are befriended and associated with the foolish.
Through mindfulness, concentration, and heedfulness, one attains the outflows-free state in succession.
By practicing tranquility and insight in each moment, one can leave behind all stains of transgression;
ego-conceit is naturally eliminated, and through liberation, one attains peace and happiness.
If a person does not sever desire, it is like leather being cast into a fire;
in an instant it is seen to be scorched and destroyed, and they shall undergo immeasurable suffering.
O Bhikṣus, be cautious regarding sensual pleasures; negligence brings much sorrow.
If one is free from craving and desire, one experiences happiness through right mindfulness.
If there is no weariness, how can there be satisfaction?
If there is no satisfaction, how can there be joy?
If there is no pleasure, what sorrow can there be?
If there is craving, what joy can there be?
With tranquility and sufficient wisdom, one is able to lengthen the path to the outflow-free.
If craving is never satisfied, one will meet an untimely death through unrighteousness.
When the mind is deluded by forms, one does not contemplate impermanence for oneself;
the fool deems them beautiful and good, unaware that they are not real.
The fool binds himself with greed and seeks not to cross to the other shore;
through craving for wealth and sensual desires, he harms others and binds himself as well.
Though the world permits many exquisite pleasures, these desires offer the least flavor.
If one were to compare the pleasures of the heavens to the *kaliśapana* hell,
even if all the mountains were made of gold like the Cakravāḍa range,
one would still find no satisfaction; the Perfectly Awakened One knows this all too well.
The bitter fruits of suffering in the world all arise from craving;
the wise who skillfully subdue it should train according to this.
When intense greed is clearly manifest, sentient beings fall into doubt and anxiety.
If one further increases the mind of craving, one creates for oneself firm fetters.
By observing well and becoming free from craving, doubts are eliminated;
by abandoning that craving and attachment, the firm fetters naturally fall away.
Enmeshed by the net of desire and shrouded by the veil of craving,
the deluded mind is bound by its own license; like a fish that has entered the hand of the fisherman,
the power of death constantly presses upon one, just as a calf follows its loving mother.
Those who are greedily attached and negligent are like monkeys encountering a fruit tree;
their greedy minds are exceedingly firm, rushing toward it again and again.
Indeed, craving provides the moisture, and conceptual thought acts as the spreading creepers.
Craving is deep and bottomless; through it, old age and death increase.
Craving is full of deception; craving harbors stinginess.
If one discerns with wisdom and observes correctly, one attains peace and happiness.
Driven by craving, they undergo birth and death, rushing forward with delight;
sentient beings lack the eye of wisdom and cannot observe for themselves.
Deluded and attached to their cravings, how could they realize they are sinking and drowning?
If one practices the yoga of meditation, the King of Māra cannot find an opportunity to strike.
The defilement of greed is difficult to dissolve; it is like a calf that loves its mother.
By abandoning greed, one avoids sinking into the depths; by abandoning greed, one attains liberation.
Through greed, strife and contention increase; through craving, slander abounds.
When a bhikṣu cultivates śamatha and vipaśyanā, he realizes the fruit of tranquility.
The greedy mind is like a fertile field; when it encounters wind and rain, it grows.
If one remains far removed from craving, afflictions cannot invade.
If desire is thin and weak, like a drop of water upon a lotus leaf, those afflictions are easily removed; such a person may be called wise.
If one cuts down a tree but does not cut its roots, though it be cut, it will grow back;
if one uproots greed but does not exhaust its root, though it be cut, it will arise again.
Greed is like cultivating a field: one must plow it to remove the weeds.
If the sprouts of craving are not weeded, the fruits of virtue will not be firm.
Greed and attachment are fundamentally no different;
since both lead to the suffering of evil deeds, why do you not feel remorse?
The nature of greed is the initial seed; the nature of craving receives the womb.
Sentient beings cling without ceasing, coming and going, difficult to escape.
All devas and human beings dwell in dependence upon craving.
Craving goes forth, followed by all fetters; it does not rest for even a single moment.
When the time has passed, sorrow arises again; only upon entering hell does one finally awaken.
Craving flows along its conditions without staying; the net of desire covers the root of the wound.
The spreading creepers increase hunger and thirst, repeatedly increasing the experience of suffering.
Just as one who fashions an arrow for oneself returns to wound their own body, so too is the internal arrow: the arrow of craving wounds sentient beings.
One who can awaken to this knows that craving and suffering arise together with existence;
being free from desire and free from the notion of existence, such a bhikṣu has truly crossed over the world.
Morality is the path to the deathless nectar; heedlessness is the road to death.
Without greed one does not die; by losing the Way, one brings about one's own ruin.
The wise person guards the Way and triumphs; they never become deluded or intoxicated.
Through non-greed one attains joy and happiness; from this, one gains the Noble Path.
Constantly contemplate and cultivate wholesome dharmas; maintain self-restraint with perpetual firmness.
The wise seek tranquility, which is the unsurpassed auspiciousness.
Like one restraining oneself from intoxication, he who can abandon it is a noble person.
Having ascended the hall of wisdom, one leaves peril behind and attains peace.
When the wise observe the foolish, they are like the mountain compared to the earth;
one should contemplate abandoning arrogance and let the wise cultivate clear wisdom.
Practicing heedfulness, restraining oneself and subduing the mind,
one can skillfully create the lamp of wisdom, whereby darkness is naturally destroyed.
When right mindfulness is constantly aroused, the mind becomes tranquil and easily extinguished [of defilements].
Self-restrained by the life of the Dharma, one does not transgress and gains a good reputation.
With focused mind, do not be negligent; practice the sage’s discipline with a disciplined mind.
Do not associate with base and defiled things, nor meet with those who are heedless.
One does not plant the root of wrong views, nor does one increase evil in the world;
with right view as the supreme path, one is scrutinized by mundane wisdom.
Having passed through hundreds of thousands of births, one never falls into hell.
Those who cultivate negligence are befriended by fools.
With calm abiding and insight undisturbed, like a master of wealth guarding his treasury,
do not crave the pleasure of strife, nor should you indulge in sensual delights.
One who contemplates with heedfulness can attain great peace;
not indulging oneself at any time, one can restrain the outflows and bring them to an end.
Heedlessness gives the Mara an opportunity, just as a lion seizes a deer.
There are four matters of negligence: First, taking pleasure in violating the wives of others;
Second, the initial [retribution] in hell; third, meager merit; And fourth, slandering and sleeping.
Lacking benefit and falling into evil, One fears and finds little joy in such pleasures.
The laws of the king impose heavy punishments; when one dies, they enter hell.

If the original intent was not to commit it, and if one knows in one's heart that one did not do it, yet disregards the path of evil and the fool still strives for it with longing—[such a person falls].
The wise are like bright lamps; those in darkness receive their light from them.
They guide the people of the world, as those with sight lead those who are blind.
If one's actions are unwholesome, they are like that person without sight.
Traversing the path is exceedingly difficult; with its perilous roads, one harbors fear.
If wholesome dharmas increase, Māra shall find no opportunity.
Realizing the extinction of outflows and attaining nirvāṇa, one may obtain the fruit of reality.
If unwholesome dharmas increase, Māra constantly watches for an opportunity;
one loses that path of tranquility and suffers without end.
As for what is called a "holder of the Dharma," it does not necessarily require much recitation or study.
If one has heard but little, yet fully practices the conduct of the Dharma-body;
though one recites and studies many meanings, if one is negligent and does not follow the Right Path,
it is like a herdsman counting another's cattle— one will find it difficult to attain the fruits of a śramaṇa.
If one hears evil and remains patient, praising those who practice the path,
eliminating greed, hatred, and delusion, one attains the state of a śramaṇa.
One should praise heedfulness and censure those who are heedless.
One will constantly obtain the rewards of humans and devas, which are supreme and most excellent.
If a person is not heedless, they will be praised by the wise;
their performed virtues will increase, and they will be able to give rise to all wholesome dharmas.
For one who acts with negligence, there is nothing that can benefit them in this present life;
when the mind is peaceful and unmoving, only then is one called wise.
A bhikṣu who maintains heedfulness avoids the many sorrows and transgressions of negligence.
Like an elephant emerging from the mud, it is difficult to rescue one from the suffering of the deep sea.
A bhikṣu who maintains vigilance will cast off the dust of all transgressions, like the wind blowing away fallen leaves; for those who are heedless, there is much sorrow and fault.
The bhikṣu who maintains heedfulness, While negligence brings much sorrow and transgression,
Is bound by the deep entanglements of the fetters, Like fire consuming dry fuel.
The bhikṣu who maintains heedfulness, While negligence brings much sorrow and transgression.
Each, following the proper sequence, attains the exhaustion of all fetters and latent tendencies.
A bhikṣu who maintains vigilance avoids the many faults of negligence;
through the analytical understanding of the meaning of the verses, he dwells in tranquility and eternal peace.
A bhikṣu who maintains vigilance, While negligence brings much sorrow and transgression,
If afflictions are eliminated, One can attain the bliss of nirvāṇa.
Without being negligent, one should initiate The cultivation of wholesome dharmas.
From this life to the next, one attains the happiness of practicing the Dharma.
Without giving rise to negligence, the afflictions are naturally subdued;
by firmly training in wholesome dharmas, one will certainly attain nirvāṇa.
One who constantly indulges in negligence finds no moment’s rest;
when life ends and they enter hell, there too is no respite for even a moment.
Negligent, they lack mindfulness and do not practice proper decorum.
Addiction to sleep is incompatible [with the path]; this is an obstacle to the precepts.
Constantly remaining free from what is incompatible prevents one’s mindfulness from being destroyed;
by maintaining constant self-mastery through mindfulness, the dust and defilements are eliminated.
A bhikṣu who maintains vigilance, upholds the precepts without violation, and skillfully guards his own mind, shall find well-being in this life and the next.
Let the bhikṣu not be heedless; having left the household life, he should follow the Buddha’s teaching.
Shake off the army of impermanence, like an elephant emerging from a lotus pond.
Relying on this Vinaya Dharma, do not harbor heedless conduct;
eliminate the wheel of birth and death, and forever attain the end of suffering.
From what is loved, sorrow arises; from what is loved, fear arises.
If there were nothing to be loved or cherished, what would there be to grieve over, what would there be to fear?
It is through love that sorrow is born; it is through love that fear is born.
If one distances oneself from mindfulness of craving, one will ultimately abandon madness and confusion.
When a person harbors grief and sorrow, the sufferings of the world become immeasurable;
this arises from mindfulness of affectionate love, for where there is no such mindfulness, there is no sorrow.
Therefore, do not give rise to thought; for thought is an evil burden.
He who is thus has no bonds; he is neither in thought nor in non-thought.
Thought is employed as a skillful means; one does not employ expedients that are contrary to the Dharma.
Through skillful means and wisdom one attains the Great Meaning, and thus reaches the state of the Supreme Honored One.
Do not associate with craving thoughts, nor dwell in the absence of such thoughts;
for through craving thoughts one does not see suffering, yet through the absence of such thoughts one falls into grief and distress.
In this state, one gives rise to sorrow and grief, which destroys one's roots of goodness.
When affection follows one into the next world, though friends and kinsmen be many, one suffers in the long night with anxiety and resentment; the thought of separation is most bitter.
Meditating on the golden hue of forms, one dwells separately with a celestial body;
yet when pleasure reaches its peak, harm arrives, and one is seized by the King of Death.
If a person, throughout day and night, eliminates thoughts of craving for form, [they shall not fall].
One who digs deep into the very root does not transcend the path of death.
One who takes an unwholesome form for a wholesome appearance, or speaks of what is unlovely as lovely—
if such a one claims to be attached to beauty, they are driven by heedlessness.
Those who harbor thoughts of desire do not dwell together with evil;
this is difficult to attain, for delight is the root of evil.
Those who would guard themselves against desire should protect themselves well.
Just as one guards a frontier city with firm walls and moats,
so too should one who wishes to care for themselves store their own person securely and closely,
just like guarding a frontier city where both the interior and exterior are made entirely firm.
One should protect oneself well; later, one will regret it in vain.
When the time has passed, sorrow arises, and in an instant, one falls into hell.
Search thoroughly in all directions to examine the state of your own mind.
Are there not those of such a kind who, having no love for themselves, yet love others?
By taking oneself as an analogy for the life of another, one therefore does not harm others.
All beings fear death; none do not dread the sword and the staff.
Use yourself as a metaphor: do not kill, do not wield the staff.
Just like a traveler who has been away for a long time, returning safely from afar, his kin and friends are peaceful and harmonious, and he returns with a heart full of joy.
Those who delight in merit and practice virtue pass from this world to the next and receive for themselves manifold blessings, just as one rejoices at the arrival of a dear friend.
Arising according to the teachings of the Most Holy One, they restrain their unwholesome minds.
Those who draw near are loved; apart from the Path, there is no true intimacy.
Whether one draws near or does not draw near, the destination in each case is different:
by drawing near to the Path, one is born in heaven; by not drawing near, one falls into hell.
One who delights in the Dharma and accomplishes the precepts, who cultivates faith and joy,
and is able to restrain themselves, will be loved and respected by others.
That they are respected by others is entirely due to what they have created within themselves.
One gains renown in the present life and is reborn in the heavens hereafter.
One should instruct others to receive [the teaching] and restrain unrighteous conduct;
this is what the virtuous keep in mind, and what the wicked should avoid.
Regarding the wholesome and the unwholesome, these two are not distinct;
the wholesome leads to rebirth in the heavens, while the unwholesome causes one to fall into hell.
The wise are able to guard the precepts, and through merit, they bring about three kinds of retribution.
One gains fame and profit in the present life, and after death is reborn in the heavens.
One should behold those who uphold the precepts and protect them as one of wisdom;
thus attaining right view, they shall find peace in this world.
Observing the precepts brings happiness; it causes the body to be free from affliction.
At night one sleeps in tranquility, and upon waking, there is long-lasting joy.
Through the precepts, one is secure until old age and death; through the precepts, one finds peace in stillness.
Wisdom is the treasure of humanity; from merit, one is hard for thieves to escape.
What dharma ultimately leads to goodness?
What dharma brings about a secure and peaceful abiding?
What dharma is the treasure of humanity?
What can no thief take away?
The dharma of precepts brings ultimate peace; the dharma of precepts brings excellent and secure rest.
Wisdom is the treasure of humanity; only merit cannot be stolen.
Cultivate precepts and practice giving; create merit as a fertile field.
From this, one reaches the further shore and always arrives at the place of peace and bliss.
The bhikṣu establishes himself in the virtue of the precepts, guarding the gates of the sense faculties;
he knows moderation in food and keeps his mind focused whether awake or asleep.
His mind constantly gives rise to awakening, and he studies with diligent effort day and night.
With a mind that clearly understands the exhaustion of outflows, one can attain the path of parinirvāṇa.
The wise establish the prohibitions and precepts, and with single-minded devotion practice wisdom;
such bhikṣus are free from feverish affliction, having exhausted the fruits of existence and eliminated all suffering.
By means of the precepts, always subdue the mind; protect the state of right concentration.
Internally train in the cultivation of śamatha and vipaśyanā; do not forget this, for it is right wisdom.
Eradicate all defilements of sin; exhaust all pride and harbor no doubt.
Throughout one's life, seek the Dharma and the precepts; do not distance yourself from noble mindfulness.
One should skillfully observe the precepts, concentration, wisdom, and liberation;
having already departed from dust and defilement, all afflictions are exhausted and will not arise again.
Accumulating pure liberation, all ignorance is utterly exhausted;
transcending the realm of Māra like the radiance of the sun,
the bhikṣu should avoid pride and delusion by staying aloof from them.
In the three practices of morality, concentration, and wisdom, Seek fulfillment and do not distance yourself from them.
Since you do not allow yourself to be self-indulgent, Do not harbor thoughts of worldly existence.
Therefore, abandon the hindrances and coverings, And such obstructions will not arise.
The bhikṣu who guards the prohibitive precepts and constantly observes those who train in them will go straight upon the path to nirvāṇa and swiftly attain such purity.
The fragrance of flowers does not go against the wind, as do the scents of the lotus and sandalwood.
The fragrance of virtue perfumes even against the wind; the person of virtue is known by their pervasive scent.
Whether it be the *ubha-varṣī*, *tagara*, or *candana*—such floral fragrances as these cannot be compared to the fragrance of ethical discipline.
If one can maintain the precepts, pure and without negligence, attaining liberation through right wisdom, this is called the state of peace and happiness.
This path is unsurpassed; it eliminates the demons of meditative concentration.
The virtue of the noble ones is immeasurable; they have attained the Eightfold Path.
Guarding against bodily misconduct, they rectify themselves and protect their own conduct.
Those who guard against bodily evil constantly cultivate wholesome bodily actions.
Guarding against verbal misconduct, One rectifies and guards one’s own speech;
He who guards against verbal faults Constantly cultivates good conduct of speech.
Guarding against mental misconduct, One rectifies and guards one’s own mind.
Guarding against evil in the mind, one should constantly cultivate wholesome mental conduct.
One should abandon evil physical conduct, as well as abandon evil verbal conduct;
one should also abandon evil mental conduct and all defiled, unwholesome dharmas.
One should cultivate wholesome conduct of the body, And likewise cultivate wholesome speech;
As for cultivating wholesomeness of the mind, Through desirelessness, one exhausts all taints.
One should cultivate wholesome conduct of the body, And likewise cultivate wholesomeness of speech and mind.
In this life and in future lives, one shall forever be born in a favorable realm.
Practicing loving-kindness and benevolence by refraining from killing, and always being able to properly restrain the body,
one attains an inexhaustible state where wherever one goes, there is no suffering.
Not committing killing is benevolence; by always being able to guard against transgressions of speech, one attains the state of inexhaustibility, and wherever one goes, there shall be no affliction.
One’s past evil karmic deeds of the body should be personally regretted and lamented.
If one is now heedful in this life, wisdom will arise and past sins will be extinguished;
regarding the evil karma of speech in the past, one should feel self-reproach and remorse—
if one does not speak falsely now, wisdom will arise and those sins will be extinguished.
One should feel remorse for past evil deeds of the mind;
now that the mind is constantly pure, wisdom arises and sins are extinguished.
Be vigilant regarding the body as one would a warrior, and be likewise vigilant regarding speech as a warrior.
Guarding the mind is heroic valor; all fetters are likewise [subdued] in this way.
This state is called the deathless; wherever one goes, there is no sorrow or affliction.
It is excellent to guard the body, and it is likewise excellent to guard the speech.
To guard the mind is good; likewise, to guard all [the senses] is so.
A bhikṣu who guards all [the senses] can reach the end of all suffering.
With mouth and mind pure, one never commits evil with the body.
To be able to purify these three types of action—this is the path taught by the Great Sage.
False speech leads one into hell; to claim "I did not do it" after having done so—one will suffer both offenses in the future, for such conduct drags one away.
Those who constantly harbor violent and evil intentions carry an axe within their mouths;
they thus wound their own bodies because of the evil words that issue forth.
One who teaches the Dharma to delight others brings forth immeasurable meanings from their mouth.
That I have conceived this body, I feel no shame for such a fate.
To praise the wicked while the wicked praise you—both of these are evil;
to delight in quarreling with the tongue leads to no peace in the end.
Vying for trivial gains is like clutching at lost treasures;
from such things arise strife and contention, leading one’s inclinations toward evil realms.
For hundreds of thousands of *Nirarbuda* hells, and thirty-six or thirty-five other prisons, [one shall suffer].
Those who slander the noble and holy, with mouth and mind uttering evil vows, fall into the evil paths through their lack of the Way, increasing their own suffering in hell.
Stay far from folly and cultivate a mind of patience; by recollecting the Truths, one will not commit transgressions.
If one relies on the inner treasure and lives according to the noble ones,
the fool falls into evil realms as if wishing for the practice of wrong views.
Having lost this present auspicious assembly, one should again establish vows and seek [the Way].
One will never perceive the Noble Truths, much less wish to see the ultimate;
just as when bamboo or reeds produce fruit they wither and destroy their own bodies, so too,
if one utters speech that is good, one will not propagate the teachings of evil dharmas.
Through goodness one attains liberation; through evil, one does not attain it.
One who is liberated through goodness is a noble person; such a one is released from the woeful realms.
The liberation of the noble ones is not like that of the foolish who attain liberation.
The bhikṣu humbles his mind; He speaks without agitation and attains loyalty.
He explains with righteousness and speaks according to the Dharma; His speech is gentle and soft.
He skillfully expounds the teaching of the noble ones; He speaks of the Dharma and speaks of the Dharma in two ways.
To speak with mindfulness is as [the first] three; to speak with truth is as [the second] four.
Therefore, one who speaks words that cause no affliction to the mind and does not harm sentient beings is one who can speak well.

To speak the truth according to the Dharma is the foundation for establishing the Path.

What is the essential departure?

Having gathered many exquisite flowers, They bind them into garlands for their hair-ornaments.
When sentient beings accumulate roots of goodness, they become increasingly distinguished in future lives.
Like the exquisite *mallikā* flower or the pure *mākula*,
when greed and hatred are eliminated, a bhikṣu is as pure and fragrant as incense.
Like one gathering exquisite flowers, with focused mind and no distraction,
Yet falling asleep and being swept away by water, suddenly he is overcome by the King of Death.
Like one gathering exquisite flowers, with focused mind and no distraction...
Sensual desire knows no satisfaction; one is constantly beset by poverty.
Like a person gathering exquisite flowers with focused and undistracted mind, yet failing to obtain true wealth and treasure, they remain long beset by poverty.
If one does not see the King of Death, with wisdom shining like a pure lotus,
the bhikṣu reaches the further shore, like a snake shedding its old skin.
When greed, hatred, and delusion are severed, it is like casting away the roots of a poisonous flower.
The bhikṣu has reached the further shore, like a snake shedding its old skin.

the bhikṣu has reached the further shore, like a snake shedding its old skin.
When the root of hatred is severed, like a flower floating upon the water,
the bhikṣu reaches the further shore, like a snake shedding its old skin.
When the root of delusion is severed, like a flower floating upon the water...
The bhikṣu has reached the other shore, like a snake shedding its old skin.
Like a person weaving a flower garland, his mind’s delight in craving knows no satiety;
failing to exhaust the poison of the present life, he is constantly bound by the three roots.
Contemplate the body as a fragile earthen vessel; illusory phenomena are like a mirage.
Severing the blooming flowers of Māra, one beholds not the path of the King of Death.
This body is like a mass of foam; know these phenomena to be illusory transformations.
Having severed the blossoming flowers of Māra, one beholds not the path of the King of Death.
With the root of self-conceit eradicated, like a flower floating upon the water,
the bhikṣu reaches the further shore, just as a snake sheds its old skin.
When the root of stinginess is severed, like a flower floating upon the water,
the bhikṣu reaches the further shore, like a snake shedding its old skin.
When the root of the branch of craving is severed, like a flower floating upon the water—

The bhikṣu has reached the further shore, Like a snake shedding its old skin.

One attains the ultimate meaning of the Dharma; Its utility is therefore inexhaustible.
Practicing harmony and patience with a single mind, one escapes the suffering of saṃsāra.
Through patience, the mind attains concentration; it can sever all afflictions.
From this, one abides in concentration, like a well-trained horse.
Having severed malice and attained the outflow-free state, like a horse that has mastered itself, one abandons evil and reaches the level plain; thereafter, one enjoys the bliss of rebirth in heaven.
Not being dissolute while among the dissolute, and awakening much while others sleep—
As a weak horse is compared to a fine steed, one who abandons evil is truly wise.
If a person possesses a sense of shame and moral dread, they can achieve wisdom;
thus they are easily led forward, like a well-trained thoroughbred urged by a whip.
Just as a horse that is well-trained and even-tempered can bear the king’s riding,
so too one who is able to train themselves is a person of excellence and receives words of sincerity and trust.
Though they are constantly disciplined, they are like a newly broken-in horse.
Even as with a well-trained elephant, one who is not self-disciplined cannot ride it;
such a person does not reach that destination which others have reached.
Only those who have disciplined themselves arrive at the place of discipline.

only one who has tamed themselves extinguishes all suffering.
That person cannot mount it, nor can they reach where others have gone.
Only those who discipline themselves will reach the path to parinirvāṇa.
One should always discipline oneself, just as one restrains a galloping horse.
Those who can restrain themselves will contemplate crossing to the far shore of suffering.
Just as King Aśoka rode his horse, so too is it rare for one to be born in that land;
a bhikṣu who is well-tamed is liberated from all suffering.
Only he who tames himself possesses a noble mind like a fine steed.
Just as the great elephant or dragon is supreme when self-tamed,
and as a king riding a wise horse is rare within his realm,
so too the bhikṣu who is well-disciplined is able to sever all fetters.
Only he who disciplines himself is supreme and peerless;
like a well-trained elephant or dragon, his mind reaches the further shore.
He is his own teacher and his own protector; seeking refuge in himself, he achieves his own deliverance.
Therefore, be personally diligent and cautious, like a merchant or a wise horse.
Eliminate anger and abandon pride; stay far removed from all afflictions.
Do not be stained by name-and-form; then enemies will have no companion.
One who has removed anger sleeps well; with anger exhausted, one harbors no grief.
Anger is the root of poison, yet for the bhikṣu it becomes sweet.
The noble ones are able to eliminate it entirely; having severed it, they sleep in peace.
When a person gives rise to a mind of anger, they perform various unwholesome deeds.
Later, when that anger is removed, the fire of wisdom gradually blazes forth.
One who lacks both shame and remorse will further delight in giving way to wrath.
Ensnared by anger, they are like those who have lost their sight in the darkness.

The powerful approach the fierce army; the powerless retreat in cowardice.

Patience is the supreme excellence; one should therefore embrace patience even toward the weak.
Both myself and the other person face a great fear from which there is no rescue;
thus, knowing that the other is angry, one should extinguish the flaws within oneself.
When both parties practice these two principles, it is so for me as it is for them.
Just as one knows the other’s anger, one should endure their faults;
when both practice these two principles, my endurance is as theirs.
The fool thinks, "I am powerless," and his view of the Dharma is likewise.
If a fool were to surpass the wise by means of coarse words and harsh speech,
and if he wished always to be victorious, he should remain silent regarding such talk.

therefore, it is said that patience is supreme among virtues.
When angry, one does not speak, remaining as if in private even when in the midst of a crowd.
A person consumed by anger never realizes it until the end;
one who speaks the truth without malice and gives with a charitable mind when asked—these three things have a fixed destination: they will naturally dwell in the celestial palaces.
When the mind is stilled, how can there be anger?
One who is self-restrained possesses clarity throughout their life; through equal wisdom and meditative liberation, having known this, they are free from anger.
If one harbors evil intentions, then for that wrath there will be the retribution of wrath.
Do not repay anger with anger; thus one overcomes the defeat of that battle.
To endure insults is to overcome resentment; the good overcome the unwholesome.
The victor is able to bestow goodness; sincerity overcomes the deceitful.
Without anger and without harming others, always mindful of true practice—
fools give rise to anger within themselves, and their enmity remains ever-present.
One should be able to restrain and sever anger, just as one stops a galloping chariot.
This is being well-tamed and controlled, departing from darkness and entering into light.
The śramaṇa and the right path; gain and loss, enmity and remembrance, purity, water and flowers; the horse, and anger as the tenth.
Having attained supreme and peerless perfect enlightenment, you are unstained by any worldly phenomena;
possessing all-encompassing wisdom, powers, and fearlessness, you are self-arisen, without teacher, and without one to be realized.

Having attained perfect enlightenment, you are most peerless; Untainted by any worldly phenomena, you possess all-encompassing wisdom, powers, and fearlessness; Spontaneously awakened, you require no teacher and have no need for a witness.
The Sugata has realized alone that which is peerless; appearing in the world, he has attained the Perfect Path.
The Tathāgata is the most honored among all devas and the world, with all supernormal powers and wisdom perfected.
I am the Buddha, the World-Honored One; having severed all outflows, I am free from lustful desire. All devas and worldlings follow my mind.
Since I have neither teacher nor protector, I am likewise solitary and without companion.
Accumulating all practices, one attains Buddhahood; naturally, one penetrates the holy path.
Having triumphed oneself, one does not receive evil;
superior to all the world, with wisdom vast and boundless, one guides the ignorant—I am the supreme victor.

The wise man does not dwell in folly; He observes the world and transforms beings accordingly.
He speaks of the stainless path, wherein there is eternal cessation beyond compare.
With the courageous lion’s roar, he whose name is Tathāgata proclaims the True Dharma;
through his teaching of the Dharma and its meaning, the Awakened One abides in eternal peace.
The courageous and steadfast establish themselves in meditative concentration; having gone forth, they extinguish [defilements] day and night.
The devas constantly provide protection, and they are praised and prophesied by the Buddha.
Among those gods and humans, he extols the Perfectly Awakened One.
Cultivating swiftly and awakening for oneself, one finally leaves behind the body born of a womb.
Speaking of all the Buddhas of the past, as well as those yet to come,
and the Perfectly Awakened Ones of the present, they largely dispel the sorrows of sentient beings.
All those who have respected the Dharma, those who do so now,
and those who shall show respect in the future— this is called the essence of the Buddha’s teaching.
If you wish to seek this essence for yourself, rectifying one's body is the foremost requirement.
Faithfully revering the True Dharma and recollecting the precepts taught by the Buddha—
those who lack faith in the Buddha are like a multitude of the blind;
they shall fall into the evil realms, like merchants who encounter a rākṣasa.
The boatman can cross the waters; diligence serves as the bridge.
Those bound by lineage and caste remain behind, while those who cross over are the brave and strong.
The Tathāgata is without equal; craving is exhausted and nothing more is accumulated.
Liberated and untainted in mind, he bestows grace upon gods and men.
Contemplating the two modes of practice and skillfully observing the two forms of seclusion,
he dispels darkness and transcends to the rank of a divine immortal, attaining mastery with ease.
Just as a person standing on a mountain peak Sees the people in the villages all around, So too is the careful observation of phenomena: Like ascending a tower to view a garden.
If one constantly observes in this way, Defilements will never arise again.
The Dharma rain of ambrosia falls, pouring down in an endless succession.
Those who have heard much and are well able to practice, cultivating goodness without affliction, find the karmic obstacles of their actions dissolved; such śramaṇas attain the wondrous fruit.
The deluded and ignorant do not perceive this; they take pleasure in practicing the way of immortality.
But for one who skillfully understands the nature of phenomena, illness is like a plantain tree.
It is just as when a house is tightly roofed over: it is dark and gloomy, and nothing can be seen.
Though there be many wondrous forms, those with eyes may not see their clarity.
It is like a person who possesses vast and extensive learning and penetrating wisdom,
yet without hearing [the teachings], they do not know what is wholesome and what is unwholesome.
Just as one holding a bright torch can see all forms and appearances, so too,
having heard [the Dharma], one is able to fully know the destinations of both good and evil.
Though such a person may be called "learned," if they are not complete in their prohibitive precepts, [they do not truly possess wisdom].
Rebuked by the Dharma and Vinaya, one’s learning is deficient;
though a practitioner may have heard little, if they are fully endowed with the prohibitions and precepts,
they are praised by the Dharma and Vinaya, even if their learning is deficient.
Though one has heard much, if one’s observance of the precepts is incomplete,
both are subject to reproach, and all that was wished for is lost.
One who has heard much and can maintain it firmly, honoring the Dharma as their wall and fence, [is truly protected].
Diligence is indestructible by praise or blame; from this, the three trainings are perfected.
One who is learned can uphold the Dharma; with wisdom, the mind is always settled.
Like that Jambu-river gold, who could say it has any flaw?
Wisdom vast constitutes great learning; when the precepts are fully and completely maintained, both bring forth renown, and all that was heard is fully attained.
Great learning is like a precious mirror, illuminating all phenomena without exception.
Illuminating oneself and illuminating others, both bring forth joy.
Like a necklace of many jewels, one first adorns oneself;
then sentient beings experience joy, their love and delight becoming inexhaustible.
Those who praise their own physical form, And those who extol their reputation and virtue— All these are forms of craving; Yet they themselves do not realize it.
To hear is to know the Dharma and Vinaya, To resolve doubts and perceive what is right.
Having heard, one abandons what is not Dharma; practicing thus, one reaches the deathless state.
Within, there is no self that knows itself; without, there is nothing seen by others.
Not seeing its fruit within, one simply dwells following the sound.
Internally one already knows it, yet externally there is nothing seen by others;
when both fruits are fully realized, one abides in accordance with sound.
Internally there is that which is known, and externally there is that which is seen.
He possesses clear wisdom and does not abide by mere sounds.
Though the ear-consciousness hears much and the eye-consciousness sees much, what is heard and seen is not firmly grasped;
matters are analyzed according to their meaning and principles.
Wisdom is firm, well-spoken, and swift; hearing and knowing with a concentrated mind is swift.
But those who do not employ wisdom and concentration, yet quickly practice heedlessness—such people find no joy in the Dharma of the noble ones, nor does their conduct accord with their speech.
Through patience one contemplates emptiness; thus the faculty of hearing becomes firm.
Constantly practicing virtuous speech, the śramaṇa reflects on sitting and rising;
finding joy in a single seat, he seeks the stilling of the mind.
Sitting alone and lying down alone, walking alone without a companion,
one should subdue one’s own mind and find joy dwelling in the mountain forests.
Even if there are a thousand or ten thousand enemies, a single man can conquer them all.
It is better to subdue one's own mind; this is victory in battle.
To conquer oneself is supreme; like those sentient beings who have subdued themselves, they become Great Beings (Mahāsattvas) and all their practices are fully perfected.
Neither a deva nor a yakṣa, neither a māra nor a Brahmā,
is superior to one who has renounced the world— the wise bhikṣu.
First rectifying oneself, one then rectifies others.
If one rectifies oneself, one is called an upper-grade practitioner.
First rectifying oneself and then rectifying others—
if one rectifies oneself, one does not violate true wisdom.
One should cultivate and discipline oneself, following its teachings and instructions;
if one has not been taught and disciplined oneself, how can one teach and discipline others?
Reflecting on self-cultivation and discipline, cause others to attain faith and understanding.
With my own mind focused and single-minded, I practice what the wise have studied.
Whether for my own sake or for the sake of others, many fail to achieve success;
yet those who learn this way rectify themselves while simultaneously instructing others.
When one’s own person remains whole and preserves the Way, how could there be room for another at that time?
Having already been brought under subjection, the wise expound its meaning:
take one's own mind as teacher, and do not follow others as teacher.
One who makes oneself one's teacher attains the Dharma of those with true wisdom.
Making one's own mind one's teacher, and not relying on another as a teacher—
one who makes oneself their teacher gains renown and attains happiness.
Take your own mind as your teacher; do not rely on others as your teacher.
One who takes their own mind as teacher attains wisdom and becomes a god among humans.
Take your own mind as your teacher; do not rely on others as your teacher.
One who makes oneself one’s teacher will long enjoy the bliss of rebirth in the heavens.
Making one’s own mind one’s teacher and not relying on another as a teacher—
one who makes oneself one’s teacher is the most excellent among kinsmen.
Take your own mind as your teacher; do not rely on another as your teacher.
One who takes their own mind as teacher has no sorrow amidst afflictions.
Take your own mind as your teacher; do not rely on another as your teacher.
One who makes oneself one's teacher cuts off all fetters.
Making one's own mind one's teacher, and not relying on another as a teacher—
one who makes oneself their teacher is able to destroy all evil realms.
Take your own mind as your teacher; do not rely on another as your teacher.
One who takes their own mind as teacher will long have true wisdom as their guide.
Take your own mind as your teacher; do not rely on another as your teacher.
One who takes oneself as teacher is liberated from all suffering.
Taking one’s own mind as teacher and not relying on another as teacher—

It is better to understand a single meaning, through hearing which one attains cessation.

It is not as good as practicing even a single verse; by practicing it, one may attain the Way.

It is not as good as for even a brief moment, observing the body and accumulating virtuous conduct.
Though one might spend a hundred years in the mountains and forests sacrificing to the fire god,
it is not as good as for even a brief moment attaining liberation through right view.
Month after month, the fool devotes himself to food and drink;
such a person who does not believe in the Buddha obtains not even one-sixteenth of the merit.
If a person prays to spirits and sacrifices, hoping for blessings throughout the year, [they gain nothing].
Among those four parts, he does not obtain even one.
Month after month, the fool consumes food and drink, yet without giving rise to a heart of compassion;
his merit is not even a sixteenth part of the other.
Month after month, the fool consumes food and drink;
yet he does not know the calculation of the Dharma, for his merit is not even a sixteenth part of one.
Month after month, if one constantly practices the assembly of equality, [the merit thereof is immeasurable].

That person who does not believe in the Dharma is not even one-sixteenth of that [merit].
Month after month, one may constantly perform equal assemblies;
yet such a person who does not have faith in the Saṅgha is not worth even a sixteenth part [of one who has].
Month after month, one may constantly perform a thousand sacrifices, always bestowing gifts with equanimity.
One who lacks a heart of compassion is not even a sixteenth part of that person.
Month after month, one may constantly perform a thousand sacrifices, always giving with equanimity;

If one performs a thousand sacrifices every month, constantly bestowing gifts with impartiality,

Month after month one constantly performs a thousand sacrifices, always bestowing gifts with equanimity;
