The merit of a single thought is boundless; it surpasses those lifelong sacrifices.
Though one should live a full hundred years, serving and making offerings to the fire god,
it would not equal even a brief moment of making offerings to the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha;
the merit of a single thought of such offering surpasses that of lifelong sacrifice.
Lacking faith and harboring hatred and envy, they incite strife between this person and that;
such people are despised and loathed by the wise, yet the foolish practice these things as their delight.
Possessing faith and free from hatred and envy, they are diligent, faithful, and possess great learning.
Respected and received by the wise, and a source of joy for the noble and holy;
one does not associate with evil friends nor join in unlawful assemblies,
but draws near to virtuous friends and constantly joins in the assembly of the True Dharma.
One who travels should be mindful and cautious; one who upholds the precepts and is learned contemplates immeasurable realms and hears those excellent teachings.
Each understands their distinctions: by associating with the evil, one sinks into ruin oneself.
Practicing goodness brings forth a good reputation;
that which is sublime remains ever sublime because of the integrity of one's person.
That which is virtuous culminates in goodness because of associating with the virtuous.
Wisdom is supreme; through upholding the precepts, one attains eternal tranquility.
Just as fish gather around putrid filth, people greedily compete to seize it;
their minds do not perceive the stench, and so it is with the habitual pursuit of evil.
When many *tagara* leaves are gathered by sentient beings, their fragrance spreads far and wide; practicing virtue is just like this.
By associating with evil friends, the stains of transgression increase day and night.
Like a pig’s body, which is impure, It defiles itself and others alike.
If one does not personally practice evil, yet associates with those who do,
One will be held in contempt by others, And an evil reputation will blaze day and night.
One practices what one observes; knowing what is near, one draws close to it.
When a poisoned arrow is within its quiver, the pure are defiled by it.
A hero can remove the defilement; having abandoned evil, he does not take it as a companion.
Therefore, knowing the fruits of retribution, the wise person discerns them all.
Do not associate with those who are not kin; rather, one should associate with the virtuous.
A bhikṣu practicing the Path endures suffering to exhaust all outflows.
Though a fool serves a person of wisdom for as long as life lasts,
he still does not understand the True Dharma, just as a ladle does not taste the food it scoops up.
A wise person, by serving a noble and holy one for even a brief moment, [attains understanding].
One by one they know the true Dharma, just as the tongue discerns all flavors.
The wise person seeks out a single phrase and brings forth immeasurable meanings;
the fool recites a thousand phrases yet does not understand the meaning of a single one.
The accomplishment of the meaning of a single phrase is what the wise cultivate and study;
the foolish prefer to distance themselves from it—this is what the True Buddha has taught.
It is better to have an intelligent enemy than to follow the counsel of a friend who lacks wisdom.
The fool is instructed in what is not the Path, and gradually proceeds along the road to hell.
When a fool calls himself a fool, one should know him to be truly wise;
when a fool calls himself wise, he is the most foolish among fools.
If one further praises the foolish and disparages the person of wisdom,
though disparaging the wise may still be superior, praising the foolish is not supreme.
Do not look upon the foolish nor hear their voices, and do not dwell together with the foolish.
It is difficult to dwell with the foolish, just as it is to live with an enemy.
Do not see the fool, do not hear his voice, and do not dwell with the fool;
it is difficult to dwell with the foolish, just as it is to live with an enemy.
When choosing with whom to dwell, one should be like meeting with one's own kin;
therefore, associate with those who are learned and who uphold the precepts.
Such people are the highest among men, like the moon among the stars.
As a tortoise withdraws its six limbs, so should a bhikṣu restrain his thoughts and intentions;
without attachment and without harming others, he attains nirvāṇa beyond words.
Patience is the supreme path; the Buddha has declared that nirvāṇa is the highest.
One should not harbor the fever of vexation, nor harm others while claiming to be a śramaṇa.
One’s speech should not be coarse or harsh; what one says should be eloquent.
If one of little learning engages in debate, one will instead suffer defeat at the hands of the opponent.
If one repeatedly gives rise to afflictions, it is like a vessel that has been shattered;
one wanders through birth and death again and again, sinking for long without hope of escape.
If one does not personally give rise to afflictions, it is like a vessel that is whole and sturdy.
Thus proceeding until one reaches parinirvāṇa, there will forever be no dust or obscuration.
Freedom from illness is the supreme benefit; contentment is the supreme wealth;
knowing true kin is the supreme friend; and parinirvāṇa is the supreme bliss.
Hunger is the foremost affliction; action is the foremost suffering.
He who knows this as it truly is, finds in parinirvāṇa the foremost bliss.
This most sublime teaching of the Noble One shall spread forth without end.
Those things commonly practiced by the world truly never bring satisfaction.
Such peerless and well-spoken instructions as these [show that] when one is oppressed by bodily suffering, what exceeds the misery of hunger?
Those who incline toward the good are few; those who incline toward evil are many.
One who knows this as it truly is should swiftly seek parinirvāṇa.
Some have the conditions to be born in a good realm; some have the conditions to be born in an evil destiny.
There is parinirvāṇa with remainder; all such things have their conditions.
As deer return to the fields and birds return to the sky, so do meanings return to conceptual analysis, and the True Person returns to cessation.
Without a lazy mind, nor reaching a state of cowardice, one who seeks parinirvāṇa shall burn away all fetters and attachments.
O bhikṣu, bale out the boat quickly; by baling it out, it shall become light.
Seeking to sever the passions of desire, one then attains parinirvāṇa.
That which I had originally does not exist; that which originally existed is now non-existent.
It is neither non-existent nor existent, and as such, it cannot be apprehended even now.
Difficult to perceive, the Truth is unshakable; well-observed, it remains unmoved.
One should examine the source of the exhaustion of craving; this is called the limit of karma.
By severing craving and eliminating desire, one dries up the river so that no sign of flow remains.
One who can clearly understand the root of this craving is said to have reached the end of suffering.
With no body, one extinguishes its perceptions; all pains attain coolness, all formations cease forever, and consciousness and perception do not arise again.
One who knows this as it truly is, is said to have reached the end of suffering.
Abiding in the movement of emptiness, one becomes still; it is neither near nor is there pleasure therein.
Through non-movement, one attains pliancy (*praśrabdhi*); through stillness, one then realizes *parinirvāṇa*.
Nor does it arise through coming and going; where coming and going cease, birth and death are ended.
With the afflictions of old age and death removed, suffering is severed and perfect nirvana attained.
I have no more coming and going; I neither depart nor arrive.
Neither perishing nor being reborn—this limit is called parinirvāṇa.
Through the arising of wisdom, one knows the beginning and end of conditioned things;
though bound by the fetters of birth and death, these bonds are difficult to restrain.

Thus, this body composed of the four great elements, a collection of the five aggregates and suffering, dwells in the contemplation of its true nature as suffering; by exhausting suffering, one attains parinirvāṇa.
All phenomena have no coming or going; coming and going are but constant arising and ceasing.
Old age, sickness, and death are ever-shifting; through the outflow-free state, one attains parinirvāṇa.
A bhikṣu may have birth in the world, performing both active and inactive deeds;
yet for one who is without birth and without existence, there is no activity and nothing to be performed.
O Bhikṣu, I have already known this: there are no further sense-bases (āyatana), no base of infinite space, no bases of sensory application, and no base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
there is neither this world nor a future world.
There is no perception of sun or moon; there is neither going nor coming.
Arising from the conditions of food, and resulting in sorrow and joy through food—when this is brought to cessation, all phenomena of suffering are exhausted.
Without food, life cannot be sustained; who then could refrain from seizing it for sustenance?
Indeed, establishing food as the priority, one subsequently attains the Way.
When the element of earth and those of water and fire are present, at that time there is no wind to blow.
Where the blazing flames do not reach, its reality is likewise unseen.
It is neither the moon nor possessed of light; it is neither the sun nor possessed of illumination.
One who observes this with discerning clarity has attained true and perfect nirvana.
With upright countenance and self-composure, one attains liberation from all suffering;
by being neither in the realm of form nor the formless, one attains liberation from the foremost suffering.
Ultimately free from fear, having transcended bonds without doubt, one stands firm.
As long as the thorn of craving for existence has not been severed, how can one know that the body is a source of suffering?
That which is called the ultimate is parinirvāṇa, the foremost;
it is the total severance of all conceptualizations and attachments, wherein words and phrases are free from error.
Knowing moderation and not knowing moderation, the Most Victorious One abandons conditioned existence and practices internal reflection, like a chick breaking through its shell.
Among all gifts, the gift of Dharma is supreme; among all pleasures, the pleasure of Dharma is highest.
Among all powers, the power of patience is supreme; the bliss of nirvana comes from the exhaustion of craving.
Skillfully observe your own flaws and ensure they do not manifest outwardly;
others have their own vulnerabilities, like the light dust that flies about.
If one claims to be without fault, yet both sin and merit arrive together;
seeing only the flaws of others, one constantly harbors thoughts of ignorance.
To know shame is the highest form of longevity; why then be bound by the pull of greed?
Those who are reckless and devoid of fear have short lives;

those who possess a sense of shame do not exhaust their lifespan. Constantly seeking pure conduct and ensuring that one’s dignified demeanor is without flaw—one should contemplate this as true, pure longevity.
The world is universally blind and enshrouded in darkness; those with the eye of wisdom are exceedingly rare.
Like flocks of birds falling into a net, being born in heaven is hardly worth mentioning.
Observing the laws of the world’s decay, one sees only the transformation of all phenomena.
The fool binds himself, entangled by darkness;
he does not see his own conditioned formations, for though he observes them, they appear as nothing.
Sentient beings all possess a self, and because of that, affliction arises.
Each does not see the other; they do not perceive the thorn of false views.
Contemplating the causes and conditions of this thorn, one sees that sentient beings are largely defiled by attachment:
"I am the creator, but that [other] does not exist; that [other] is the creator, but it is not mine."
Sentient beings are entangled by pride; Stained and attached to arrogance, They are deluded by views, And cannot escape the bounds of birth and death.
Those who have already attained and those who shall attain— Both alike receive the dust and defilement.
Having mastered the root of illness and awakened to all that is to be learned,
one observes those who maintain the precepts— those whose holy life is pure—
and attends to those who are sick and frail; this is called reaching the ultimate limit.
One should contemplate them as bubbles upon water, And likewise contemplate them as a mirage;
If one does not view the body in this way, One will not perceive death approaching.
One should contemplate them as bubbles upon water, And likewise contemplate them as a mirage.
Thus, by not regarding the world, one does not see the King of Death.
One should contemplate the body in this way: like a king’s multicolored chariot, upon which the foolish become stained and attached; one should skillfully seek to distance oneself from it.
Thus one should contemplate the body: like a king’s multi-colored chariot, it is that to which the foolish are attached, while the wise keep far from it.
Thus one should contemplate the body: as the source of all diseases.
When sickness and folly meet, how can one rely upon them?
One should contemplate this painted image with its mani-jewel-like deep blue hair;
yet the fool takes it as a causal support and does not seek to cross to the further shore.
One should contemplate this painted image with its mani-jewel-like deep blue hair;
the fool takes it as a causal support, while the wise person regards it with revulsion.
It is forcibly adorned with colors and forms, yet it is but a body of loathsome impurity.
The fool takes these as objects of attachment, yet seeks no means for his own deliverance.
Dividing the nails and hair into eight parts, and the earrings from the two ears—
these are what the fool becomes stained by, yet he seeks no means for his own deliverance.
Attached to desire and stained by desire, one does not investigate the conditions for the fetters;
yet without giving rise to those fetters, one should cross over the flood of sensual existence.
Not freed from the garden while remaining in the garden, one who has been freed from the garden returns once more to the garden.
One should further observe this person: having been freed from bonds, they are again subjected to them.
Now, having renounced the throne of a heavenly king, he does not create the root of birth and death;
seeking liberation from the suffering of hell, he prays for you to speak of the bliss of parinirvāṇa.
Clad in blue garments with a white parasol, the charioteer drives his single-wheeled chariot;
seeing those who have not yet left behind defilement, he seeks the opportunity to sever their fetters and attachments.
Many people seek refuge in mountains, rivers, trees, and spirits.
Seeking refuge in gardens, groves, or divine shrines in hopes of escaping suffering and calamity—
this is not the supreme refuge, nor does it bring auspiciousness.
Those who take refuge in such things shall not be liberated from all suffering.
If there are those who take refuge in the Buddha, And in the Dharma and the Saṅgha of Bhikṣus,
Practicing the Noble Four Truths as they are seen by wisdom—
That suffering arises from the causes and conditions of suffering— They shall transcend this root of suffering.
The Noble Eightfold Path leads to the cessation of suffering and the realm of the Deathless.
This is the supreme refuge; it is not without benefit.
For those who take this refuge, they shall be liberated from all suffering.
Having observed, one should observe; not having observed, one should also observe.
Having observed, one observes again; having observed, one does not observe again.
Observing and observing again, one discerns the fundamental nature of that [object].
Calculating day as night, the precious body will soon perish.
Beholding without repeated observation, though seeing, one does not see;
like seeing yet not seeing, one observes and still does not see.
What is seeing and what is not seeing?
What is it that speaks of seeing and not seeing? By reason of what do we speak of seeing and not seeing?
Because one gives rise to views by not contemplating suffering,
one should always deeply contemplate oneself in order to understand the root of suffering;
this is called sublime and wondrous contemplation.
Who causes ordinary persons not to contemplate the root of all conditioned phenomena?
By observing through that [root], one leaves behind darkness and perceives the great light.
Do not commit any evil deeds; practice all wholesome deeds.
To purify one’s own mind through practice—this is called the teaching of all Buddhas.
By practicing generosity one obtains the reward of merit;
by harboring no resentment or anger, one uses the good to extinguish evil, leaving no trace of desire, hatred, or delusion.
Walk alone and do not follow the foolish; if you wish to associate with others, follow the wise.
The wise eliminate their own evil, just as a crane selects milk from water to drink.
Observing the manifold transformations of the world, they know the traces of phenomena arising and ceasing.
The noble and wise do not delight in the world; the foolish do not dwell among the wise.

Understanding that mindfulness awaits the flavor [of the Dharma], and contemplating the meaning of rest, one is free from fever and the thought of hunger; one should partake of the flavor of the Dharma.
If a person does not damage their mind, nor corrupt their intent,
using goodness to eternally extinguish evil, they need not fear following the paths of woe.
If a person wishes to refine their spirit, they must cultivate and polish it repeatedly.
The wise are easily refined and adorned; they are called the heroes of the world.
Those who can draw near to them find peace and freedom from sorrow;
forever stilled and without fault, they are gentle and not impetuous.
Blowing away all evil dharmas, like the wind falling its leaves;
Fearing those people without cause who slander and defame the pure—
They soon encounter the power of their own evil, like smoke and clouds driven by the wind.
Whether a person performs good or evil, each knows it for themselves:
by cultivating good one obtains good fruits; by committing evil one follows the path of suffering.
Having realized what is pure and what is impure within oneself, why worry about the purity of others?
The fool does not refine himself, like iron striking pure steel.
If one sees with the eye what is not wrong, the clever person seeks skillful means;
the wise live well in this world and do no evil.
The merchant on the road is fearful; with few companions and much merchandise, as he passes through perilous places, he has cause for anxiety that his axle might break.
If one possesses no sores upon the body, one will not be harmed by poison.
Poison cannot do anything to a scar;
when there is no evil, nothing is created.
Those who commit many evil deeds will surely bring suffering upon themselves.
To bestow gifts and spread benevolent virtue—this is exceedingly difficult.
How admirable are those who cultivate goodness! How lamentable are those who commit great evil!
For the wicked, doing evil is easy; for the wicked, doing good is difficult.
The fool considers himself upright, yet his evil remains unripened;
when his evil has fully ripened, all manner of sufferings likewise ripen.
The wise man perceives evil and does not allow himself to be ripened by it.
As with evil that is not yet ripe, the wicked observe their own wickedness;
the virtuous observe their own wickedness until the virtue is not yet ripe.
But when virtue has reached maturity, the virtuous observe one another’s virtue.
Though a person may commit evil deeds, they should not do so repeatedly;
they should take no pleasure in them, knowing that evil brings suffering.
A person who is able to perform meritorious acts should likewise create them again and again.
If one desires and takes pleasure in that state, one will cherish its karmic rewards.
First, one must restrain the virtuous mind and subdue the roots of evil;
from this, one gives rise to meritorious deeds, whereas the mind otherwise delights in evil.
Though the evil one commits may be slight, the suffering he undergoes in future lives is profound;
yet when he attains boundless merit, it is as if poison were removed from his heart and belly.
Though the merit one performs may be minute, the great fortune and virtue one receives in the future are vast.
One shall obtain a great fruit and reward, just as one reaps the reality of what was sown.
To treat the faultless with contempt and to invade the non-hostile with aggression—
one shall, for ten lifetimes, surely go to those realms.
Painful itching and coarse speech—this body will surely decay;
oppressed by manifold ailments, the mind is distracted and unsettled.
Kinsmen are parted and scattered, and wealth and goods are exhausted and spent.
Plundered by bandits, their wishes do not accord with their intent;
or again, through countless transformations, they are consumed by fire.
With their bodies destroyed and lacking wisdom, they likewise proceed to the ten realms.
Commit no evil and do not say there is none; if one commits evil and says there is no sin, or hides in a secluded corner and says there is no sin, there will surely be evidence and proof of this.
Commit evil and you shall speak of sorrow; having committed it long, you shall likewise speak of sorrow.
One grieves for the hidden corners, and one grieves for that retribution;
grieving here and grieving there, one grieves for both evil deeds.
One grieves for what one has done and receives the retribution for it; only by observing one's conduct does one come to know this clearly.
This one rejoices and that one rejoices; both rejoice in meritorious deeds.
That one performs the deed and that one receives the retribution; seeing the deed, one’s own self is purified.
This one suffers and that one suffers; both suffer for evil deeds.
He who cooks shall receive the retribution; the efficacy of one's actions is seen within oneself.
By performing merit and not committing evil, all proceeds from the law of past deeds.
One will ultimately fear not the path of death, like a boat crossing a current.
The light of the night illuminates the darkness until the sun has risen;
once the sunlight spreads its great brilliance, the light of the night becomes dark and dim.
So too, when the Observer spreads his radiance, before the Tathāgata has appeared, [the world is shrouded in gloom].
The Buddha emits a great radiance, Where there is no examination and no śrāvakas.
To conceive the notion of solidity in the non-solid, Or the notion of non-solidity in the solid—
In the end, one does not reach the state of solidity, Because of having given rise to false views.
One who knows the firm as firm, and the not-firm as not-firm, seeks that which is truly firm;
such a person takes right practice as the foundation.
The fool, however, regards [worldly things] as firm, and is consequently bound by the nine fetters.
Like a bird caught in a net, this is due to the depth and firmness of craving.
Those who harbor doubts regarding this world and the world beyond can extinguish them all through meditative concentration; free from affliction, they cultivate the holy life.
Free from dust and detached from defilement, one who can wear this robe has no driver and reaches nowhere; this is not the robe of the Dharma.
Cultivating precepts, equanimity, wisdom, and concentration, one should contemplate karma.
This one ought to wear the kāṣāya;
though his reputation reaches far and his countenance is pleasant, he harbors a mind of craftiness and hypocrisy.
Only one who can sever this [defilement]— [is fit for the robe.]
Permanently uprooting its very foundation.
The wise remove all impurities; thus they are said to possess "excellent form.
They do not indulge in physical appearance, but discern the intentions of others upon a mere glance.
The world is full of those who act contrary to the Dharma, wandering through the world like counterfeit brass that contains nothing but copper within.
They wander alone without fear or restraint; their inner nature is foul and their outward appearance is impure.
Greedily devouring without self-restraint, one revolves through the three realms according to the seasons;
like a pig kept in a pen, one undergoes the womb again and again.
If a person can concentrate their mind and know moderation in eating, [they shall not suffer thus].
Seeking to support their physical forms, they nourish their lives while guarding their path;
though observing purity, they remain self-purified.
Yet they have no satiety regarding food—such are the practices of the common folk.
If sensual desires further increase,
one should contemplate the practice of impurity; with the sense faculties free from deficiency or leakage,
one should know moderation in eating.
Possessing faith and diligence, one does not indulge in the desires of the mind;
like the wind blowing against Mount Tai, such a person finds great joy in solitude. Yet people do not delight in that place;
it is where the desireless dwell, not the abode of those possessed by desire.
Difficult to shift and difficult to move, like those heavy snow-capped mountains;
they do not appear to the unvirtuous, just as one cannot see a target shot at night in a dark room.
There may be thousands of virtuous people, yet the wise are rare among the multitudes.
The principles are extremely profound, discerned by the wise.
Among the many classes of sentient beings, most do not encounter them, as if failing to hit a mark;
yet now, observing these principles, those who lack precepts feel ashamed.
Observing existence, one knows fear; seeing change, one knows the absence of permanence.
Therefore, do not delight in existence; you should resolve to be far removed from it.
Lacking faith and lacking gratitude, they break through walls to commit theft.
One who has severed that longing for thought is called a hero.
Having removed the conditions of parents, the royal family, and the two types [of kin],
and having utterly extinguished their spheres of influence, one practices the stainless holy life.
If a person has no basis of reliance, And knows that which is most esteemed by them—
emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness— They take these into contemplation as their practice.
Just as a bird flies through the void, Yet leaves no trace of its path behind.
Like those who practice in this way, their speech has no objective referent.
Those who can sever the root of existence do not rely on what is yet to come;
they take emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness as the objects of their contemplative practice.
Rare indeed are sentient beings; most do not accord with their own nature.
Among those who are to be saved and those who are not, it is exceedingly difficult to bring about their cessation.
For all that exists, there is the teaching of equality; one should contemplate each phenomenon in relation to all others.
Having completely severed all fetters and latent tendencies, there is no longer any feverish distress.
On the path, there is no more sorrow; throughout the day one attains liberation.
When all fetters and latent tendencies are exhausted, there is no longer any manifold affliction.
Just as a bird flies through the sky without being obstructed,
so too that person attains the outflow-free concentrations of emptiness, signlessness,
and wishlessness. Just as a bird flies through the sky without being obstructed...
The practitioner reaches the other shore through the concentrations of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
There is no creating and no one who creates; the creator suffers afflictions.
Neither creating nor not creating, one grieves before and grieves after.
The doer acts with skillful excellence; having acted, he harbors no grief.
Acting joyfully and acting well, he is born in heaven to receive bliss.
As there are no tracks in the sky, so the śramaṇa has no outward intent.
All people delight in evil, yet the Buddha alone is pure and free from defilement.
As the void leaves no tracks, so the śramaṇa has no outward intent;
all in the world is impermanent, and for the Buddha there is nothing that belongs to a self.
All gods and worldlings, through practicing all [wholesome] deeds,
shall attain liberation from all suffering and, free from craving, escape the cycle of saṃsāra.
All gods and worldlings, through practicing all [wholesome] deeds...
One who can distance themselves from all evil karma will not fall into the miserable realms.
Furthermore, one who does not know the treatises makes no distinction between the wise and the foolish;
yet if one understands the meaning of the treatises, what they speak leaves no trace of defilement.
One who speaks discourse in accordance with the Dharma should raise the banner of the ṛṣis;
the Dharma-banner is the ṛṣi, and the ṛṣi is the Dharma-banner.
Some may revile him in silence, while others may revile him in the midst of the assembly.
There may be those who revile one even before they have spoken; in this world, there is no one who does not revile.
Whether it be a single instance of disparagement or a single instance of praise, these serve only to profit one's reputation.
Since neither existence nor non-existence can be truly established, such things are ultimately unknowable.
Praised by the wise, whether for beauty or even for ugliness, the wise person is without flaw;
through wisdom and concentration, they attain liberation.
Like purple-polished pure gold, they are thoroughly purified within and without.
Just as Mount Sumeru is not moved by the wind,
so too is the wise person not moved by blame or praise.
Like a tree that has no root, how could there be branches, let alone leaves?
The steadfast one has untied his bonds; who could destroy his virtue?
Stainless and dwelling nowhere, he has planted the seeds of suffering within the trench of the body.
Most supreme and free from craving, gods and men do not know him.
Like a forest of nets, when there is no craving, how could there be anything else?
The Buddha possesses immeasurable practices; since there is no track, whose track would he follow?
If one does not desire birth, then through birth one does not undergo existence.
The Buddha has immeasurable practices; being traceless, who can follow his traces?
If one wishes to extinguish all conceptualization, there will be no causes within or without, nor any transgressions regarding the perception of form;
thus, the four [elements] shall not lead to further birth.
Abandoning what precedes and abandoning what follows, Abandoning the interval, one transcends existence;
When all is completely abandoned, One no longer undergoes birth and old age.

Chapter 30: On Joy, from the *Udānavarga* (Verses on the Essential Collection of Dharma). Victory breeds enmity; self-exaltation brings self-contempt.
To still the mind is true happiness, where there is neither victory nor defeat.
If one disturbs others while seeking peace and happiness for oneself,
one will instead become their enemy and never attain liberation.
Delighting in sensual pleasures, they strike at living beings with staves.
Seeking one's own peace therein, one will find no happiness in future lives.
If a person desires joy and happiness, they should not lay a staff upon living beings;
by seeking their own happiness therein, they shall also find happiness in future lives.
Delight in the Dharma and delight in its practice; be careful not to practice unwholesome dharmas.
Those who are able to practice the Dharma well find happiness in this world and the next.
Those who protect the Dharma and practice the Dharma cultivate it and obtain a favorable retribution.
This accords with the teaching of the Dharma and Vinaya; practicing the Dharma, one does not go to evil states.
One who guards the Dharma and practices the Dharma is like a canopy covering its form;
this accords with the teaching of the Dharma and Vinaya; practicing the Dharma, one does not go to evil states.
Evil conduct leads to hell; one’s rebirth falls into the evil realms.
Through unrighteousness, one sinks into ruin, like a hand grasping a venomous snake.
If both the righteous and the unrighteous were to receive the same retribution, there would be no distinction between the two.
Through unrighteousness one enters hell; through the True Dharma one is born in heaven.
To compare giving with battle is something that the wise and virtuous do not praise;
for in both the time of giving and the time of battle, these two matters are exactly equal.
When a person encounters hundreds of thousands of changes, they who equally eliminate the enemy of pride, bestow a pure mind at the proper time, and are steadfast—such a man is most excellent.
A little patience gains more than much [anger]; virtue conquers much sloth.
Those who possess faith and wisdom in giving receive good retribution in future lives.
Through the meritorious reward of giving, all that one wishes for is fully accomplished;
one swiftly attains the foremost cessation and gradually enters the realm of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
If one seeks skillful means and bestows the wisdom of the noble ones, exhausting the very root of suffering, know that one shall obtain a great reward.
Loving the Dharma brings peace and security; the mind becomes pure and stainless.
The Dharma taught by the noble ones is that which the wise delight in.
If a person’s heart finds joy in dhyāna, they likewise find joy in non-arising,
find joy in the four foundations of mindfulness, as well as the seven factors of enlightenment.
As well as those four bases of spiritual power, The eightfold path of the noble ones,
Delighting in solid food, Delighting in wearing the dharma robes,
Delighting in walking meditation, And delighting in dwelling among mountains and thickets.
Having attained the state of peace, one is unconditioned in the present life.
Having transcended all fears and surpassed all worldly attachments,
one delights well in mindfulness and maintains it well, skillfully contemplating all phenomena.
Excellent is the one who harms none in this world, who nurtures all classes of living beings;
who is free from worldly desire and attachment, who has transcended all defiled attachments,
and who is able to extinguish their own pride— this is called the foremost happiness.
The joy of the elders who uphold the precepts; the joy of those perfected in faith;
the joy of discerning the meaning and purpose; the joy of not committing various evil deeds;
the joy of having parents in this world; and the joy of a harmonious assembly.
In the world there is the joy of the śramaṇa; the joy of one whose will is tranquil is likewise so.
There is the joy of the appearance of the Buddhas; there is the joy of being able to receive the teaching of the Dharma.
There is the joy of the harmony of the Saṃgha; when there is harmony, there is constant peace.
The joy of perfecting the precepts; the joy of extensive learning and broad knowledge.
The joy of beholding the True Person; the joy of the path leading to liberation.
The joy of the cool, pure waters of virtue; the bliss of the wealth of Dharma gathering of its own accord.
Attaining the clarity of wisdom brings joy; extinguishing pride and being free from evil brings joy.
To behold the virtuous is blissful, and to assemble with them is likewise joyful.
Not associating with fools brings enduring and perpetual joy.
Do not associate with the foolish for even a single day;
living together with the foolish is as difficult as meeting those one hates.
Living together with the wise is as easy as meeting one's own kin.
A person of wisdom is extremely rare to encounter; their birth is never in vain.
Wherever they may take birth, that family will surely receive blessings.
All shall attain peace and security as the Brahmin attains parinirvāṇa.
Untainted by desire, one is completely liberated from all sense bases;
having utterly severed inauspicious fetters and subdued internal afflictions,
one attains eternal rest and sleep, and the mind-consciousness becomes perfectly clear.
Be careful not to cling to pleasure; you should instead protect your future conduct.
You should contemplate renouncing the world and observe the nature of joyful things.
Whether it be the delights of worldly desires or the pleasures of the heavens—
This is called the ultimate limit of craving; in sixteen [rebirths], not even one has been attained.
Those who wish to cast off the heavy burden and no longer create heavy karma—this heavy burden is the suffering of the world—to be able to renounce it is the greatest happiness.
Having completely severed all cravings and extinguished all conditioned formations, as well as the root of the five aggregates, one will no longer undergo rebirth in the three realms of existence.
In the accumulation of meaning there is joy; friends partake in the bliss of merit.
That cessation is tranquil bliss, spreading and reaching all people.
Suffering has bliss as its root, just like a brazier of blazing fire that,
though fiercely burning, gradually subsides until it is extinguished.
Not knowing where they converge—such people who possess such views are freed from the mire of craving and desire; when they depart, they have no fixed location.
Having attained the bliss of immovability, there is no anger within them.
There is change and no staying still; remove sorrow and there will be no grief.
Contemplate the world in silence: where there is joy, there is no affliction.
One who hears much of the True Dharma, even if they see some loss, remains untroubled.
Everyone craves for form; there is no worldly life-span without fetters.
One who understands the source of the Great Dharma should clearly perceive the defects of these fetters.
The minds of all people are bound and attached, and they are likewise bound by the root of form.
All who suffer humiliation, all who indulge their own whims—
victory and defeat arise naturally, yet in the end nothing is gained.
Those who desire pleasure and long life should be able to endure such slighting retribution.
The one who practices patience endures others, yet cannot endure dwelling within the realms of existence;
those who seek pleasure and long life remain undeluded regarding delusions.
While the deluded are confused by others, I am here without such delusion.
Those who wish to attain happiness and long life, and who are ultimately free from all fetters,
should subsist on the food of mindfulness. Like those gods of the Ābhāsvara Heaven,
who constantly take mindfulness as their food, their minds and bodies shall not be consumed by the fires of affliction.
Sentient beings perceive suffering and pleasure, yet the Noble Dharma remains undestroyed;
though they encounter the traces of contact, where there are no traces, how can there be contact?
Like a bhikṣu in meditative concentration, he is not attached to any defilements.
Sentient beings encounter suffering and pleasure, yet they are unable to perceive them.
The Tathāgata, the learned one, oneself, the extensive, the virtuous friend,
parinirvāṇa, contemplation, and the karmic obstacles— these correspond to the tenth [chapter] on happiness.
The mind is light and difficult to subdue; it dwells within the embrace of desire.
To subdue the mind is good; through such subduing, one attains serenity.
It is like a fish on dry land, having been removed from the deep abyss.
The mind-consciousness is filled with extreme dread, and the hosts of Māra flee in all directions.
The mind runs to many places, like the radiance of the sun;
yet it can be restrained by the wise, just as a hook stops a rogue elephant.
Now I discourse upon this mind, which is without solidity and invisible;
I now wish to instruct you, so be careful not to create any flaws.
Let not your mind wander, nor indulge itself in negligence.
I now restrain you once more, like one who tames a wild and unruly elephant.
Birth and death are without measure; coming and going have no beginning.
Those who seek a dwelling place undergo the womb again and again.
Having observed this dwelling, one no longer constructs further houses;

seeing that the beams and rafters have decayed and the towers and pavilions have collapsed, the mind has already detached from all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*); within this interval lies one's own mind.
The mind is for the most part fickle and restless; it is difficult to sustain and difficult to guard.
The wise are able to rectify it themselves, just as a craftsman straightens an arrow by pressing it.
When there is anger, one knows there is anger; when there is anger, one knows that there is anger.
This mind is created by oneself; it is not the work of one's parents.
Abandoning the heterodox to settle in the orthodox, cultivate merit without turning back.
If a roof is not made watertight, rain will constantly leak through.
If a person does not practice reflection, they will constantly experience lust, anger, and delusion.
Just as rain will always leak through a house if the roof is not sealed tight,
if a person practices reflection, they will forever be free from lust, anger, and delusion.
The mind is the root of all phenomena; the mind is sovereign and the mind is the driver.
If the mind conceives of evil deeds, they immediately manifest as speech and action.
Suffering follows one’s own transgressions just as the wheel follows the track of the chariot.
The mind is the root of all phenomena; the mind is the master and the mind is its messenger.
If the mind conceives of wholesome conduct, then one speaks and acts accordingly;
blessings and joy will follow of their own accord, just as a shadow follows its form.
Not with an impure mind, nor toward those who are angry,
should one wish to know the Dharma taught by the Perfectly Awakened One.
Those who have eliminated arrogance and whose minds are utterly pure— [to them it is revealed].
Only by being able to relinquish thoughts of harming others can one hear the True Dharma.
If the mind does not abide in stillness, one will neither know wholesome dharmas nor possess correct knowledge and vision regarding supramundane matters.
The thirty-six currents of defilement, along with the outflows of mind and intention,
repeatedly give rise to wrong views based on the fetters of sensual desire.
Abandoning the mind and letting go of its roots, a person turns and revolves according to their own will.
To diminish one's reputation, like a bird abandoning an empty forest,
dwell in tranquility and practice self-cultivation; be careful not to follow the tracks of desire,
lest you swallow a hot iron ball and wail as you suffer its retribution.
One should practice what ought to be practiced, yet relies on strength instead of diligent effort;
thus one sinks into the lowliness of human form, being indolent and failing to understand wisdom.
Both distracted observation and right observation are both produced by the mind.
One who can awaken to and contemplate the mind finds that the foolish mind is repeatedly distracted.
When the wise contemplate in this way, the mindful practitioner acts with single-minded dedication;
alas, when the mind is free from attachment, only a Buddha can extinguish this [defilement].
Contemplate the body as an empty jar; settle the mind like a fortified city.
With wisdom, wage war against Māra, and having secured victory, do not lose it again.
Contemplate the body as a mass of foam, as a mirage, or as a wild horse of the desert.
With wisdom, wage war against Māra; guard your victory and do not lose it again.
Contemplate the seven factors of enlightenment with an even mind, without deviation;
you should abandon deluded thoughts and delight in the patience of non-arising.
Having exhausted all outflows and being free from taints, one attains parinirvāṇa in this world;
one should guard one’s own mind as a wild ox guards its tail.
By bestowing gifts upon all, one shall never be parted from happiness.
One dragon emerged from among the dragons, the six-tusked one among them all.
With a mind ever equal toward itself, he alone found joy in the vast wilderness;
never harboring a harmful intent, he acted entirely for the sake of all people.
One who practices loving-kindness for all sentient beings harbors no resentment.
One who practices loving-kindness for even a single person thereby protects the roots of all goodness.
This should be done for all; such is the supreme merit praised by the noble and the wise.
Universally loving all beings, Compassionately mindful of the various classes of sentient beings,
One who practices a mind of loving-kindness Will later receive unsurpassed bliss.
If one acts with a leaping spirit, Rejoicing without indolence,
By cultivating all wholesome dharmas, one attains the state of peace and security.
One brings joy to oneself through the harmony of body, speech, and mind;
having attained equal liberation, the bhikṣu finds bliss in the cessation of mental activity.
All fetters are exhausted, and there is no further defilement;
even the music of the five instruments cannot gladden the mind.
It is not as good as a single upright mind directed toward the Dharma of equanimity.
The Most Excellent One has attained the excellent eye, and yet does not conceive of a self.
Those with minds that delight in dhyāna do not delight in sensual desires;
the Most Excellent One’s mind leaps with joy, and yet he does not perceive a self.
Those who possess a mind that delights in meditation and does not delight in sensual desires,
whose fetters are forever exhausted, are as immovable as a mountain.
They are unstained by passion and do not give rise to anger toward those who provoke it.
Those who possess such a mind— how could they know the traces of suffering?
Harmless and unstained, fully endowed with the precepts,
they know moderation in food as well as in bedding and seating.
Cultivating the mind and seeking skillful means— this is called the teaching of all Buddhas.
When the practitioner contemplates the characteristics of the mind, discerning thoughts and awaiting the settling of the will,
they thereby enter meditative concentration and immediately attain joy and peace.
Guarding the mind is one's own adornment; being jealous of others while striving for oneself, one encounters sorrow yet suffers no affliction—the wise abide in careful discernment.
When a person does not guard the mind, they are harmed by false views.
Those who harbor thoughts of restlessness and frivolity will follow the path to death.
Therefore, one should guard the mind, practice pure conduct with equanimity,
keep right view ever before oneself, and discern the phenomena of arising and ceasing.
The bhikṣu who has subdued sleep, having exhausted suffering, shall not create it again;
he who has subdued his mind finds joy and guards his heart so that it does not wander.
Sentient beings, led astray by their own minds, undergo all the sufferings of hell.
To subdue the mind brings joy; guard the mind and do not let it wander again.
Guard the mind and do not let it wander again; the mind is the gateway to all wonders.
By guarding it so that nothing is lost, one abides in the path of parinirvāṇa.
If a bhikṣu goes for alms, he should not accumulate what he has obtained;
thus praised by gods and men, he is born pure and free from blemish.
A bhikṣu, out of compassion, should love and revere the Buddha’s teaching.
Deeply entering sublime *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, one extinguishes defiled conduct and finds peace.
When a bhikṣu has exhausted all cravings, having abandoned craving and cast off arrogance,
and being without self while eliminating the notion of "I," who would not be close to this truth?
Know that this practice of the Dharma is the essential path for the body;
like an elephant contending with a powerful enemy, the bhikṣu should constantly practice it.
Before a person’s life-span is exhausted at the end of the kalpa, they must strive within to contend with their own mind.
Guarding oneself, mindful of the Truths of the Path, the bhikṣu dwells in pure peace.
Mindful of kin as if they were friends, maintaining a livelihood that is upright and unadulterated;
knowing what should be given and when it should be given, he is likewise endowed with dignified conduct.
A bhikṣu who is equipped with all practices is able to reach the end of suffering;
delighting in the Dharma and desiring the Dharma, he contemplates the Dharma of peace and security.
A bhikṣu should act in accordance with the Dharma, maintaining it correctly without neglect or forgetfulness.
One should train in entering the concentration of emptiness; a bhikṣu should always remain tranquil.
Delighting in non-human abodes, one observes the dharma of equality;
one should restrain the five aggregates and control the mind like flowing water.
Pure and ever harmonious and joyful, one drinks the flavor of nectar.
Like a most precipitous mountain, unmoved by the wind,
the bhikṣu who has exhausted all delusion is not shaken wherever he may be.
All names and forms are non-existent; do not give rise to delusion.
If you do not draw near, you will have no attachment; only such a one is called a true bhikṣu.
A bhikṣu is not defined by shaving his hair; one who is arrogant and lacks the precepts is not a bhikṣu.
One who abandons craving and contemplates the Path is truly a bhikṣu.

It is not merely shaving the hair that constitutes a "pacified mind"; one who is free from negligence, possesses resolve and faith, and can extinguish all suffering and affliction is a supreme great śramaṇa.
The bhikṣu who attains the concentration of loving-kindness, Who receives and upholds the teachings of all Buddhas,
And has fully realized the path of total cessation— Do not look upon him with attachment, even though he is dear to you.
With a heart full of joy and supreme gladness, He further becomes one who possesses mindfulness.
The bhikṣu is full of joy; throughout the void, there is no root or source.
He quiets the body and quiets the mind; he restrains his speech and is likewise virtuous.
Having renounced the world as a bhikṣu, he crosses over suffering without hindrance.
Without dhyāna there is no wisdom; without wisdom there is no dhyāna.
The Path arises from dhyāna and wisdom, leading one close to the way of perfect peace.
Practice dhyāna without negligence; do not allow your mind to be disturbed by desire.
Do not swallow molten copper, which brings self-affliction and scorches the physical frame.
One who can protect one's own body and speech, guarding the mind so that no evil arises,
and subsequently attains the dharmas of the precepts, is therefore called a bhikṣu.
All who cultivate wholesome dharmas take the seven factors of enlightenment as their foundation;
this is called the sublime Dharma, and thus one is named a bhikṣu established in concentration.
As is now being taught, one knows for oneself the source of the exhaustion of suffering.
This is called the root of virtue; such a one is a bhikṣu free from outflows.
Not by the power of observing precepts, nor by the meaning of extensive learning, nor even by attaining a concentrated mind, does one become attached to literary embellishment.
When a bhikṣu has something to rely upon, he brings his untainted conduct to completion;
he should contemplate the bliss of perfect awakening and not draw near to ordinary worldlings.
Contemplating the phenomena of this present life, he analyzes the five aggregates.
While practicing the path, do not commit evil; you must resolutely restrain your own mind.
Having left the home life to attain liberation, if the mind remains stained by attachment and one’s practice is lax and slack, then the weariness of such a mind will not be dispelled.
If one does not purify their conduct, how can they attain great wealth?
When the mind finds eternal rest, and the bhikṣu restrains the activities of the mind,
he brings an end to old age, sickness, and death, and is thereby liberated from the bonds of Māra.
The mind has attained eternal tranquility; the bhikṣu who restrains his mental activity has brought an end to old age, sickness, and death, and shall no longer undergo further existence.
Having severed the marks of craving, the bhikṣu who restrains his mental activity—
Having brought an end to old age, sickness, and death, one shall no longer undergo further existence.
With a mind free from fetters and defilements, the bhikṣu who restrains his mental conduct has brought an end to old age,
sickness, and death, and shall no longer undergo further existence.
Unable to sever the root of existence, though a bhikṣu restrains his mental activities,
he will not escape old age, sickness, and death, nor will he no longer undergo further existence.
But able to sever the roots of the three poisons, a bhikṣu who restrains his mental activities [will attain liberation].
Having brought an end to old age, sickness, and death, one shall no longer undergo further existence.
Having escaped the realm of Māra and triumphed over the thorns of the forest,
and having removed those who revile, one remains like Mount Sumeru.
The bhikṣu does not experience suffering, nor does he dwell on this world or the next;
viewing the world as like an illusion or a dream, the bhikṣu transcends both.
Like a snake shedding its old skin, he is able to sever the root of craving.
Having exhausted the deep spring of desire, the bhikṣu triumphs over both sides.
Like a snake shedding its old skin, he who can sever the five desires and cut off the very root of craving— the bhikṣu triumphs over both sides.
Like a snake shedding its old skin, One who can sever the five fetters And pull out the thorn of craving—
Such a bhikṣu transcends both this world and the next.
Like a snake shedding its old skin, He has no worldly attachments among all realms of existence.
Furthermore, having severed the unwholesome roots, the bhikṣu excels over both [this world and the next].
Like a snake shedding its old skin, he is free from the feverish afflictions of existence.
Furthermore, having severed the unwholesome roots, the bhikṣu excels over both.
Like a snake shedding its old skin, He severs desire without remainder;
Like pulling out what is not firmly rooted, The bhikṣu triumphs over both worlds.
Like a snake shedding its old skin, He cuts off the arising of craving as it flows forth.
Like a snake containing venomous poison, the bhikṣu excels both.
Like a snake shedding its old skin, he who has severed all conditioned perceptions and does not harbor such thoughts within his mind— the bhikṣu excels both.
Like a snake shedding its old skin, If the root of greed is utterly severed,
He is called a true bhikṣu, Who has subdued the armies of Māra.
Having attained the end of the wheel of saṃsāra, If the root of hatred is utterly severed...
This is called a true bhikṣu, liberated from all afflictions.
Having attained the end of the cycle of suffering, if the root of delusion is severed and exhausted,
this is called a true bhikṣu, far removed from all fetters.
Having brought the cycle of suffering to an end, If the root of pride is severed and exhausted,
One is called a true bhikṣu, Capable of being free from attachment and defilement.
Having brought the cycle of suffering to an end, If stinginess is severed and exhausted,
This is called a true bhikṣu, who has faith and delight in the Perfectly Awakened One.
Having attained the exhaustion of the cycle of suffering—the thorn of the village of craving—a bhikṣu should reflect: "If I can distance myself from that."
The Buddha said that a true bhikṣu regards the mind of anger as a thorn in the village;
a bhikṣu should reflect upon this so as to be able to abandon hatred.
The Buddha said that a true bhikṣu regards the mind of delusion as a thorn in the village.
A bhikṣu should reflect: "If one is free from delusion, the Buddha calls him a true bhikṣu. Pride is a thorn in the village;
a bhikṣu should reflect: "If one can abandon arrogance..."
The Buddha said that a true bhikṣu is one who regards stinginess as a thorn in the village;
a bhikṣu should reflect on this so that he may be able to abandon stinginess.
The Buddha said that a true bhikṣu is one who has subdued thoughts of craving and attachment.
Just as medicine neutralizes snake venom, so can a bhikṣu destroy it;
like a snake shedding its old skin, he who subdues thoughts of anger is like medicine neutralizing snake venom— so can a bhikṣu destroy it.
Just as a snake sheds its old skin, Subduing thoughts of ignorance,
And just as medicine neutralizes snake venom, The bhikṣu is able to remain far removed [from them].
Just as a snake sheds its old skin, Subduing thoughts of pride,
Just as medicine neutralizes snake venom, so can a bhikṣu remain far removed from it;
like a snake shedding its old skin, he subdues thoughts of stinginess.
Just as medicine neutralizes snake venom, so can a bhikṣu remain far removed from it.
Just as a snake sheds its old skin, if greed should arise within you, cut it off like a reed; the afflictions are as deep as the ocean.
A bhikṣu should be diligent; if anger should arise within you, [cut it off likewise].
Cut them down like reeds; the afflictions are as deep as the ocean.
A bhikṣu should be diligent; if delusion should arise within him, he must cut it down like reeds, for the afflictions are as deep as the ocean.
A bhikṣu should be diligent; if arrogance should arise within him, he must cut it off like reeds, for afflictions are as deep as the ocean.
A bhikṣu should be diligent; if stinginess should arise within him, [he must sever it].
Cutting through [defilements] like reeds, the afflictions are as deep as the ocean.
A bhikṣu should be diligent; one who upholds the precepts is called a bhikṣu.
Only by realizing emptiness does one practice dhyāna; practicing emptiness, one investigates its source.
The unconditioned is the supreme bliss; the bhikṣu endures what causes him sorrow.
Discerning his bedding and requisites, he should practice with heedfulness, severing craving for existence without remainder.
One who is called a *brahmin* is not merely one who goes naked, dwells in dangerous places, or lies upon thorns; such a person is not named a *brahmin*.
One who has cast off the body and relies on nothing, and does not recite the words of heterodox teachings—[he is a *brahmin*].
One who has completely eliminated unwholesome states is called a brahmin.
One who cultivates pure causes in this life will have no defiled fruits in the next;
one who does not practice any unwholesome states is called a brahmin.
If one relies on no sensual desires, and the mind has no attachment,
having abandoned [the world] and attained what is right— this is called the extinction of the suffering of the end.
Those who rely on nothing and constantly practice right view,
One who constantly contemplates the exhaustion of all outflows is called a brahmin.
The fool merely accepts shaggy hair, along with beds and bedding;
harboring a mind of greedy attachment within, what does he seek by outward adornment?
Wearing tattered and coarse clothing, personally receiving and practicing the good Dharma,
dwelling in seclusion and reflecting within— this is called a brahmin.
Seeing the ignorant and foolish coming and going, falling into the moat and suffering affliction, [he feels compassion].
Desiring to cross alone to the further shore, taking no pleasure in the speech of others,
but solely extinguishing evil so that it does not arise— he is called a brahmin.
Having cut off the stream and already crossed over, free from desire like Brahmā, he is a brahmin.
One who acts with wisdom to exhaust all taints—such a person is called a brahmin.
Not by water is one purified; though many bathe themselves, it is one who can eliminate base and evil dharmas who is called a brahmin.
One is not a śramaṇa by shaving the head, nor is one called a practitioner of the holy life (brahmacarya) merely by claiming it;
if one can extinguish all evils, then such a person is a true seeker of the Way.
By practicing non-duality, they are pure and free from blemish.
One who has severed all bonds and attachments is called a brahmin.
To leave the household life for the holy life, to enter the right path as a śramaṇa,
and to abandon all defiled conduct— this is what is meant by "leaving home."
One who has no deluded mind, no pride, no doubt,
no craving, and no notion of self— such a person is called a brahmin.
I do not call one a brahmin merely because they were born from parents.
When one has extinguished those many defilements, they are a brahmin.
When body, speech, and mind are pure and free from fault,
and one is able to restrain these three types of conduct, such a person is called a brahmin.
When seeing others revile or strike one another, To receive it silently without giving rise to anger,
Possessing the power of great patience— Such a person is called a *brahmin*.
If one sees others encroaching or deceiving, One should simply mindfully maintain the practice of the precepts.
One who keeps the body upright and is self-subdued is called a brahmin.
Regarding what the world calls good or evil, long or short, large or small—
one who neither grasps nor rejects these is called a brahmin.
Being the very root of wholesome conduct, with speech and mind free from transgression,
one who can accomplish these three sublime states is called a brahmin.
Not rejoicing at coming, nor grieving at departing— this is the teaching of the Buddhas.
One who should distance themselves from the crowd is called a brahmin.
Having severed affectionate ties, having left the home life free from desire—
if craving has been exhausted, one is called a brahmin.
When one goes to that, there is no "that"; even that which goes to each "that" does not exist.
One who has abandoned craving—such a person is called a brahmin.
When one goes to that, there is no "that"; that which goes to each "that" is empty.
Untainted by the three evil states, he is called a brahmin.
One who can renounce domestic affairs, uproot the source of craving and desire,
and being free from greed, knows contentment— he is called a brahmin.
Now, having exhausted all that is known and investigated the very limit of the source of suffering,
one who no longer possesses the heart of desire and attachment is called a brahmin.
Regarding both evil and merit, both paths should be forever abandoned.
Free from sorrow and free from defilement— such a one is called a brahmin.
Having forever eliminated both evil and merit through these two paths,
and being unstained by attachment in the three realms— such a one is called a brahmin.
Just as a needle pierces a mustard seed through many petals of flowers,
one who is not defiled by desire is called a brahmin.
With a joyful mind free from dust and stain, he is like the full, radiant moon.
One who has utterly eliminated slander and defamation is called a brahmin.
Like the moon, clear and bright, suspended in the void,
one who is untainted by sensual desire is called a brahmin.
Avoiding dispute, one does not dispute; provoked, one does not become resentful or angry;
responding with kindness to those who act with malice—such a person is called a brahmin.
Deeply understanding subtle wisdom, he discerns the right path from the wrong.
One who has realized the supreme meaning is called a brahmin.
Among all those people in the world who subsist by begging,
he who is without self and without attachment does not lose the conduct of a brahmin.
One who speaks of wisdom that is boundless is called a brahmin.
If one can abandon sensual desire, leave the home life, and relinquish all sensations,
thereby severing the outflows of desire, such a person is called a brahmin.
One who has compassion for sentient beings, causing them no fear, who is non-violent, beneficial, and virtuous—such a person is called a brahmin.
One who avoids enmity remains without enmity; one who does not inflict injury remains unharmed.
One whose inclinations are toward what is deviant and perverse—this is called a brahmin.
One for whom there is nothing before, nothing after, and nothing in between;
one who has no grasping and no relinquishing in their conduct—this is called a brahmin.
One who has removed lust, anger, and delusion, along with pride and all evil deeds—like a needle passing through a mustard seed—is called a brahmin.
A city is made secure by its moats; those who enter and leave it must endure suffering.
One who wishes to reach the further shore should not accept the words of others;
only he who can extinguish [defilements] so they do not arise is called a brahmin.
One who is able to sever craving for both this world and the next—
One whose craving has been exhausted is called a brahmin.
A sentient being who has no expectations for this world or the world beyond—
because they have nothing to expect— is called a brahmin.
One who does not know their own consciousness, yet can know the immeasurable contemplations of devas, humans, and yakṣas—him we call a brahmin.
I take refuge in the Honored One among men; I take refuge in the Supreme One among men.
I do not know, World-Honored One, by means of what dhyāna you have attained this;
I pray that the God among Gods will expound its teachings and precepts.
You yourself recognize past lives and behold the paths of gods and humans.
Knowing the end of birth is the source of suffering, with a mind of wisdom forever extinguished;
knowing for oneself that the mind is liberated, freed from desire and without attachment;
having already accomplished the three knowledges—such a person is called a brahmin.
One who knows their own past lives, understands the causes and conditions of sentient beings,
and has awakened to non-attachment like the Tathāgata— such a person is called a brahmin.
Having completely severed all fetters, they are likewise free from burning affliction.
The Tathāgata has awakened to non-attachment; he is called a brahmin.
The supreme among sages and dragons, the most honored of great seers, bathed by countless Buddhas—he is called a brahmin.
With all afflictions exhausted, having crossed the stream and become free from outflows,
one who has thus transcended to the other shore is called a brahmin.
A bhikṣu wearing robes made from cemetery rags contemplates that sensual desires are not real.
Sitting in the empty and secluded place beneath a tree— this is called a brahmin.
If a person has no conscious awareness, no speech, and no discourse,
and their body is cold without warmth— this is called a brahmin.
Having abandoned all conditions and left the household life, one goes forth without fear and is able to partake of the taste of the nectar of immortality; such a person is called a brahmin.
Having severed the affairs of the world, their speech is free from harshness and coarseness.
One who scrutinizes the Eightfold Noble Path is called a brahmin.
One who travels far and wanders alone, who remains hidden without form or shadow,
and who, being difficult to subdue, has mastered self-discipline— he is called a brahmin.
Formless and invisible, this too is invisible;
he who understands this phrase has a basis for his mindfulness.
When one realizes that the fetters are exhausted, such a person is called a brahmin.
One who can sever the river of birth and death, who can endure and transcend the world, and who has awakened by himself to escape the moat of suffering—him we call a brahmin.
One should seek to cut off the flow and cross over; such a brahmin is free from desire.
One who internally observes all the sensory faculties is called a brahmin;
one who can know this is indeed called a brahmin.
Having first learned to eliminate their mother, they lead the king and his two ministers.
One who has completely transcended all sensory realms is called a brahmin.
Those who understand the profound Dharma do not inquire whether one is old or young;
they carefully maintain their precepts and faith, like a brahmin who performs fire-sacrifices.
Among those outside their own teachings, the brahmin is supreme;
all taints have been exhausted without remainder.
Or again, regarding all phenomena, they have been exhausted without remainder.
Or again, one contemplates their convergence, seeing that all is exhausted and nothing remains;
or again, one contemplates their causes and conditions, seeing that all is exhausted and nothing remains.
Just as with the fundamental nature of internal phenomena, the brahmin abides in the external.
If one shares a bed and mat with another, like that *bakkula* [fruit],
it is just as the inner nature is fundamental while the Brahmin remains on the surface;
knowing birth, knowing old age and sickness, he further knows the path of death.
The sun shines upon the day; the moon shines upon the night;
armor and weapons shine upon the army; meditation shines upon the practitioner of the Way.
When a Buddha appears, he illuminates the world, able to light up all darkness.
The brahmin possesses none of these; though there is sorrow, he has no thought of it.
Like a wish-fulfilling gem that turns according to one's will, he extinguishes doubt in every instance.
Giving rise to all profound dharmas, the brahmin practices and enters meditative absorption.
Able to unravel the net of doubt, he personally knows its suffering.
Producing all profound dharmas, the brahmin practices and enters meditative absorption,
illuminating the entire world like the sun in the sky.
The birth of all profound dharmas; The brahmin practices and enters dhyāna, Able to resist the enemy Māra, Just as the Buddha is freed from all defilements.
Protecting the mind and the bhikṣu; The Chapter on the Brahmin is at the end.
Expounded according to their respective chapters, these are complete in thirty-two [sections].
Thus ends the *Dharmapada-gāthā-saṃgraha* compiled by the Venerable Dharmatrāta.
